source_text: Ἐπὶ δὲ τούτοις τεθαῤῥηκότες, οὐ μεῖον ἢ τοῖς ἤδη γενομένοις, καὶ τὴν ἑαυτῶν ἐπισκοποῦντες φύσιν, τήν τε μετ᾿ ἐνδείας καὶ φθορᾶς ζωὴν στέργομεν, ὡς τῷ παρόντι βίῳ προσήκουσαν, καὶ τὴν ἐν ἀφθαρσίᾳ διαμονὴν ἐλπίζομεν βεβαίως· ἣν οὐ παρ᾿ ἀνθρώπων ἀναπλάττομεν μάτην, ψευδέσιν ἑαυτοὺς βουκολοῦντες ἐλπίσιν, ἀπλανεστάτῳ δὲ πεπιστεύκαμεν ἐχεγγύῳ, τῇ τοῦ δημιουργήσαντος ἡμᾶς γνώμῃ, καθ᾿ ἣν ἐποίησεν ἄνθρωπον ἐκ ψυχῆς ἀθανάτου καὶ σώματος, νοῦν τε συγκατεσκεύασεν αὐτῷ καὶ νόμον ἔμφυτον ἐπὶ σωτηρίᾳ καὶ φυλακῇ τῶν παρ᾿ αὐτοῦ δεδομένων, ἔμφρονί τε βίῳ καὶ ζωῇ λογικῇ προσηκόντων, εὖ εἰδότες ὡς οὐκ ἂν τοιοῦτον κατεσκεύασε ζῶον καὶ πᾶσι τοῖς πρὸς διαμονὴν ἐκόσμησεν, εἰ μὴ διαμένειν ἐβούλετο τὸ γενόμενον. Εἰ τοίνυν ὁ τοῦδε τοῦ παντὸς δημιουργὸς ἐποίησεν ἄνθρωπον ἐπὶ τῷ ζωῆς ἔμφρονος μετασχεῖν, καὶ γενόμενον θεωρὸν τῆς τε μεγαλοπρεπείας αὐτοῦ καὶ τῆς ἐπὶ πᾶσι σοφίας τῇ τούτων συνδιαμένειν ἀεὶ θεωρίᾳ, κατὰ τὴν ἐκείνου γνώμην καὶ καθ᾿ ἣν εἴληχε φύσιν, ἡ μὲν τῆς γενέσεως αἰτία πιστοῦται τὴν εἰς ἀεὶ διαμονήν, ἡ δὲ διαμονὴ τὴν ἀνάστασιν, ἧς χωρὶς οὐκ ἂν διαμείνειεν ἄνθρωπος. Ἐκ δὲ τῶν εἰρημένων εὔδηλον ὡς τῇ τῆς γενέσεως αἰτίᾳ καὶ τῇ γνώμῃ τοῦ ποιήσαντος δείκνυται σαφῶς ἡ ἀνάστασις. Τοιαύτης δὲ τῆς αἰτίας οὔσης, καθ᾿ ἣν εἰς τόνδε παρῆκται τὸν κόσμον ἄνθρωπος, ἀκόλουθον ἂν εἴη τὸν τούτοις κατὰ φύσιν ἢ καθ᾿ εἱρμὸν ἑπόμενον διασκέψασθαι λόγον· ἕπεται δὲ κατὰ τὴν ἐξέτασιν τῇ μὲν αἰτίᾳ τῆς γενέσεως ἡ τῶν γεννηθέντων ἀνθρώπων φύσις, τῇ δὲ φύσει τῶν γενομένων ἡ τοῦ ποιήσαντος ἐπὶ τούτοις δικαία κρίσις, τούτοις τε πᾶσι τὸ τοῦ βίου τέλος. Ἐξητασμένων δὲ ἡμῖν τῶν προτεταγμένων ἐπισκεπτέον ἑξῆς τὴν τῶν ἀνθρώπων φύσιν.
pass_a_gloss: Having been established on these things, we no less than those which have already happened, and examining our own nature, we love the life which is with need and corruption, as being suitable to the present life, and we hope for the abode in incorruption surely; which we do not fabricate in vain beside men, feeding ourselves with false hopes, but we have trusted in the unfailing pledge, the mind of the one who created us, according to which he made man from an immortal soul and body, and constructed a mind for him and an innate law for salvation and the keeping of the things given by him, for a life and a logical life being suitable, knowing well that he would not have constructed such a living being and adorned it with all things for abiding, if he did not want the thing that came to be to abide. If therefore the creator of this universe made man for the purpose of sharing in a life of intelligence, and having come to be, a spectator of his grandeur and the wisdom over all things, to co-abide with these things in contemplation always, according to his mind and the nature he has taken, the cause of generation is a guarantee of abiding forever, and abiding is a guarantee of resurrection, without which man would not abide. It is clear from the things that have been said that the cause of generation and the mind of the one who made it clearly show the resurrection. Since the cause is such, according to which man has been brought into this world, it would be logical to examine the argument which follows from these things naturally or by consequence; and in examination, the nature of the generated men follows from the cause of generation, and the just judgment of the one who made them follows from the nature of the things that have come to be, and the end of life follows from all these things. Having examined the things previously arranged, we must next examine the nature of men.

choices.english: for the purpose of sharing in a life of intelligence
choices.why: to convey the idea of participating in a rational life
to convey the idea of a natural consequence
to indicate the next step in the argument

pass_b_english: Confident on this ground, we cling to our present life, flawed and needy though it is, just as those who went before us did, while we also look forward with certainty to an incorruptible existence. That hope is no human invention, no empty wish we feed ourselves; we rest on the unshakable pledge of our Creator's purpose. He fashioned us from an immortal soul and a body, gave us a mind and an inborn law to preserve the gifts He granted, so that we might live a rational, well‑ordered life. He would never have built such a being and equipped it with every capacity for endurance unless He intended it to last. Therefore, since the Maker of all things created humanity to share in an intelligent life, to become a spectator of His majesty and of the wisdom that governs all things, and to remain forever in that contemplation according to His will and the nature He assigned, the very fact of our creation guarantees perpetual endurance, and endurance guarantees resurrection — without which humanity could not endure at all. From what has been said it is clear that both the cause of our generation and the mind of our Maker plainly prove the resurrection. Because the cause is of this sort — the reason humanity was brought into this world — it follows that we must examine the argument that naturally or logically flows from it. In that examination, human nature follows from the cause of generation, the Maker's just judgment follows from the nature of what He has made, and the goal of life follows from all of these together. Having considered the preceding points, we must now turn to the nature of human beings.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the complex causal structure of the Greek text, particularly the relationship between 'cause of generation' (τῆς γενέσεως αἰτία), 'mind of the maker' (τῇ γνώμῃ τοῦ ποιήσαντος), and the resulting 'resurrection' (ἀνάστασιν). Pass A and Pass B are consistent with the Greek source.
